name: Rome
tagline: Three thousand years of history, served with perfect carbonara
description:
Rome wears its three thousand years lightly. You can sip an espresso beside a temple that has stood for nearly two millennia, cut through a Baroque piazza on your way to lunch, and watch Vespas weave past ruins that once framed an empire. The layers are everywhere: medieval towers on ancient foundations, Renaissance palaces built from stone scavenged off the Colosseum.

Beyond the headline sights, the city is intensely lived-in. Trastevere's ivy-hung lanes fill with diners after dark, Monti mixes vintage boutiques with wine bars, and Testaccio remains the heartland of old-school Roman cooking, where the famous pasta quartet of carbonara, cacio e pepe, amatriciana and gricia is treated as scripture.

Pace yourself. Summer afternoons are fierce, so rise early for the ancient sites, retreat for a long lunch, and re-emerge for the evening passeggiata when the stone glows gold. Toss a coin in the Trevi, drink from the free public fountains and let yourself get lost, because in Rome a wrong turn usually leads somewhere wonderful.

safety.notes: Rome is generally safe, but pickpockets target crowded buses to the Vatican, Termini station and the Trevi Fountain crowds. Ignore anyone pressing 'free' bracelets or roses on you, and keep bags zipped and in front.

tipping: Tipping isn't expected and a small 'coperto' cover charge is often added, but rounding up or leaving a few euros for good service is appreciated.
gettingAround: The historic center is best explored on foot, with two useful metro lines plus buses and trams filling the gaps; tap a contactless card at metro gates and on most buses. Take taxis only from official ranks or book them through an app.
tips: Refill your bottle at the nasoni, the free cast-iron fountains on nearly every corner; block the spout with a finger and water arcs up from a hole on top for easy drinking.
Colosseum tickets are issued in your name and checked against ID; they release about a month ahead and the arena and underground slots sell out first.
Walk two streets away from any major sight before choosing a restaurant, since picture menus and touts are a reliable sign to keep moving.
Carry a light scarf: St. Peter's and many other churches turn away anyone with bare shoulders or knees.
At busy coffee bars, pay first at the register, then hand your receipt to the barista; standing at the counter is always cheaper than sitting.
Many state museums are free on the first Sunday of the month, but queues are brutal, so use it for smaller sites like the Baths of Caracalla rather than the headline attractions.
etiquette: Sitting or eating on monuments like the Spanish Steps, or wading in fountains, can earn a hefty on-the-spot fine.
Say 'buongiorno' when entering a shop, switching to 'buonasera' from mid-afternoon.
Cappuccino is a morning drink; order an espresso after lunch or dinner as Romans do.
Dinner rarely starts before 20:00, and lingering at the table for hours is expected rather than rude.

neighborhoods.name: Centro Storico
neighborhoods.blurb: The tangle of lanes around the Pantheon and Piazza Navona, packed with Baroque churches, espresso bars and splashing fountains.

neighborhoods.name: Trastevere
neighborhoods.blurb: Ivy-draped lanes, buzzing piazzas and a dense cluster of trattorias just across the Tiber.

neighborhoods.name: Monti
neighborhoods.blurb: One of Rome's oldest residential quarters, now a village of vintage shops, wine bars and cafés a short walk from the Colosseum.

neighborhoods.name: Testaccio
neighborhoods.blurb: Working-class and proud, home to a superb covered food market and the birthplace of many classic Roman dishes.

neighborhoods.name: Prati
neighborhoods.blurb: Elegant, orderly boulevards beside the Vatican with good shopping and far fewer tourists after dark.

dishes.name: Cacio e pepe
dishes.description: Just pecorino romano, cracked black pepper and starchy pasta water whipped into a glossy sauce; deceptively simple and devilishly hard to perfect.

dishes.name: Carbonara
dishes.description: Egg yolks, crisp guanciale, pecorino and black pepper, and never cream, as any Roman will gladly tell you.

dishes.name: Supplì
dishes.description: Fried rice croquettes filled with tomato-rich risotto and a molten mozzarella core that stretches like a telephone cord when you bite in.

dishes.name: Carciofi alla giudia
dishes.description: Whole artichokes twice-fried until the leaves turn crisp as potato chips, a Roman-Jewish specialty at its best in spring.

dishes.name: Maritozzo
dishes.description: A soft, sweet brioche bun split open and stuffed with a cloud of whipped cream, the classic Roman breakfast indulgence.

events.name: Natale di Roma
events.description: Rome marks its legendary founding on April 21 with parades of costumed legionaries and special openings at ancient sites.

events.name: Feast of Saints Peter and Paul
events.description: On June 29 the city honors its patron saints with a public holiday, a papal Mass and fireworks over Castel Sant'Angelo.

events.name: Festa de' Noantri
events.description: Trastevere's centuries-old neighborhood festival brings a Madonna procession, food stalls and music to the riverside lanes.

events.name: Rome Film Festival
events.description: Red carpets roll out at the Auditorium Parco della Musica, with public screenings, talks and star appearances across the city.

attractions.name: Colosseum
attractions.description: The largest amphitheater the Romans ever built still stuns, its tiered arches once packed with some 50,000 spectators roaring at gladiator bouts and wild-beast hunts. Upgrade to a ticket that includes the arena floor or the underground hypogeum to see the tunnels and lifts that hoisted animals into the daylight.
attractions.hours: 08:30 to one hour before sunset (to about 19:15 in summer)
attractions.bookingTip: Name-specific tickets release about 30 days ahead on the official site, and arena and underground slots sell out first, so book the moment they open.

attractions.name: Roman Forum
attractions.description: Once the bustling heart of the empire, this valley of broken columns, triumphal arches and temple steps is where senators debated and Julius Caesar was cremated. Climb the adjoining Palatine Hill for shady gardens, imperial palace ruins and a sweeping view back over the whole Forum.
attractions.bookingTip: The standard Colosseum ticket also covers the Forum and Palatine for 24 hours, so visit the Forum while the amphitheater queue is at its longest.

attractions.name: Pantheon
attractions.description: Nearly 1,900 years old and still capped by the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome, the Pantheon is ancient Rome's best-preserved building. Stand beneath the open oculus and watch a disk of sunlight creep across the coffered ceiling; when it rains, drops fall straight through to tiny drains in the marble floor.
attractions.bookingTip: You can pay the small fee on the spot, but a timed ticket booked online skips the midday queue under the portico.

attractions.name: Trevi Fountain
attractions.description: This Baroque showpiece bursts out of a palace wall in a tumble of sea gods, rearing horses and cascading travertine. Tradition says a coin tossed over your left shoulder guarantees a return to Rome, and the thousands of euros collected each week go to charity.
attractions.hours: Visible 24 hours; ticketed basin-side access during the day
attractions.bookingTip: A small fee now applies to the viewing area beside the basin during daytime hours; come before 9am or late at night to enjoy it without the crush.

attractions.name: Vatican Museums
attractions.description: Miles of galleries hold the popes' treasures, from classical marbles like the Laocoön to Raphael's frescoed rooms, before the grand finale of Michelangelo's Sistine Chapel ceiling. Talking and photos are banned in the chapel, so find a spot along the side benches and simply look up.
attractions.hours: 08:00–19:00 Mon–Sat (last entry 17:00); closed Sun except the last Sunday of the month
attractions.bookingTip: Book the first entry slot online several weeks ahead, or look for the summer Friday evening openings when crowds thin dramatically.

attractions.name: St. Peter's Basilica
attractions.description: The mother church of Catholicism is built to overwhelm, with Bernini's twisting bronze canopy, Michelangelo's heartbreaking Pietà and a nave so vast that floor markers show where lesser cathedrals would end. Climb to the dome for a view straight down Via della Conciliazione to the Tiber.
attractions.bookingTip: Entry is free but the security line can top an hour by 10am, so arrive at opening with shoulders and knees covered; the dome climb is ticketed separately.

attractions.name: Galleria Borghese
attractions.description: A cardinal's summer villa crammed with some of the most breathtaking sculpture on earth, including Bernini's Apollo and Daphne, where marble seems to sprout leaves before your eyes. Caravaggio's canvases hang nearby, and the surrounding Villa Borghese park is perfect for a stroll or a rowboat afterward.
attractions.bookingTip: Entry is only by pre-booked two-hour slot, and weekend slots often sell out weeks in advance.

attractions.name: Trastevere
attractions.description: Across the Tiber, this former working-class quarter of ochre houses, ivy curtains and cobbled lanes is Rome at its most photogenic. Mornings are sleepy and local around the market at Piazza di San Cosimato, while evenings see trattorias spill onto the streets and buskers gather before the golden mosaics of Santa Maria in Trastevere.
attractions.bookingTip: Reserve dinner ahead on weekends, and wander south of Viale di Trastevere for quieter, more local tables.

attractions.name: Campo de' Fiori
attractions.description: By day this lively square hosts a colorful market of produce, spices, pasta and flowers; by night it becomes one of the old center's busiest drinking spots. The brooding hooded statue of the philosopher Giordano Bruno, burned here in 1600, keeps watch over it all.
attractions.bookingTip: Come before 11am for the best stalls, then walk two minutes to Piazza Navona or the Jewish Ghetto for lunch.

attractions.name: Janiculum Hill
attractions.description: The highest lookout in central Rome unrolls a panorama of domes and bell towers stretching all the way to the Alban Hills. A cannon fires from just below the terrace every day at noon, and on weekends the park hosts an old-fashioned puppet theater for kids.
attractions.bookingTip: Walk up from Trastevere via the steps of Via Garibaldi, pausing at the monumental Acqua Paola fountain, or take bus 115 on hot days.

hotels.name: Palazzo Lucerna Trevi
hotels.description: A 17th-century noble palace two lanes from the fountain, restored with frescoed ceilings, marble baths and a rooftop terrace where aperitivo comes with a skyline of domes. The concierge arranges after-hours tours and chauffeured drives along the Appian Way.

hotels.name: Corte dei Glicini Trastevere
hotels.description: Fourteen rooms wrap a wisteria-draped courtyard on a quiet lane, with terracotta floors, linen bedding and vintage maps of Rome on the walls. Breakfast is served under the vines with ricotta tarts from the bakery next door.

hotels.name: Ostello Lupa Monti
hotels.description: A sociable hostel in a converted 19th-century apartment block, a ten-minute walk from the Colosseum, with air-conditioned dorms and a roof terrace. Nightly communal pasta dinners cost next to nothing and are the easiest way to make friends.

hotels.name: Hotel Travertino Pinciano
hotels.description: Mid-century Italian furniture, honeyed travertine and bold contemporary art fill this sleek hotel on the edge of the Villa Borghese park. There's a compact spa with a plunge pool, and bikes wait at the door for rides through the gardens.

hotels.name: Foresteria dei Pellegrini
hotels.description: A former pilgrims' guesthouse in the medieval Borgo, where vaulted corridors lead to calm rooms, some with views of St. Peter's dome. The cloister garden is a rare pocket of silence a few steps from the Vatican crowds.

hotels.name: Terrazze Giubbonari Apartments
hotels.description: Self-catering apartments above a busy shopping street between Campo de' Fiori and the Jewish Ghetto, each with a kitchen for cooking your market finds. Top-floor units share a rooftop terrace wrapped in jasmine.

restaurants.name: Lumina Gianicolo
restaurants.description: A glass-walled dining room on the slopes of the Gianicolo, where the city's domes glow beyond the candlelight. The chef reworks Roman classics into delicate courses, such as carbonara reimagined as a single silky egg-yolk raviolo.
restaurants.signatureDish: Egg-yolk raviolo with guanciale and pecorino

restaurants.name: Trattoria Da Nando e Gilda
restaurants.description: Paper tablecloths, family photos on the walls and a husband-and-wife team who have been tossing cacio e pepe in the same pans for decades. Order fried artichokes in spring and the oxtail stew year-round, with house wine by the carafe.

restaurants.name: Teglia & Tegola
restaurants.description: Long-fermented Roman pizza sold by weight and scissored to order, with toppings that swing from potato and rosemary to mortadella and pistachio. It's ideal fuel before or after the Vatican crowds, eaten standing on the sidewalk.
restaurants.signatureDish: Pizza bianca with potato and rosemary

restaurants.name: Caffè Oculus
restaurants.description: A narrow marble-topped bar where locals knock back an espresso in under a minute while pastry cooks fill cream-stuffed maritozzi to order. It sits a few steps from the Pantheon yet is priced for Romans rather than tourists.

restaurants.name: Sora Ester al Portico
restaurants.description: Deep-fried artichokes opened like golden flowers are the star at this handsome trattoria near the ancient Portico d'Ottavia. The menu draws on centuries-old Roman-Jewish recipes, from crisp salt-cod fillets to a ricotta and sour-cherry tart.

restaurants.name: Osteria Tre Archi
restaurants.description: A cozy Monti osteria where the amatriciana is rich with crisp guanciale and the Colosseum is a five-minute stroll away. Locals come back for the saltimbocca and a short list of natural wines from the Lazio hills.

restaurants.name: Nishiki Rasella
restaurants.description: When you need a break from pasta, this lantern-lit izakaya pours sake and Japanese craft beer alongside gyoza, yakitori and slurpable ramen. Counter seats let you watch the grill cook at work.

restaurants.name: Gelateria Nocciola Nera
restaurants.description: Small-batch gelato made from Piedmont hazelnuts, Sicilian pistachios and seasonal fruit, kept in lidded steel tins rather than piled into fluffy mounds, which is the sign of the real thing. Take a cone into the Villa Borghese gardens for a perfect afternoon.

experiences.name: Beneath the Arena: Colosseum Underground Small-Group Tour
experiences.description: Descend into the hypogeum's maze of tunnels and animal pens, then step onto the reconstructed arena floor where gladiators once fought. An archaeologist guide continues through the Forum and Palatine Hill, bringing the ruins to life with stories of emperors and ordinary Romans.

experiences.name: Sfoglia & Mattarello: Fresh Pasta and Tiramisù Class
experiences.description: Shop the Campo market with a Roman home cook, then roll, cut and shape fettuccine and ravioli by hand in a vaulted kitchen nearby. The session ends with a long lunch of everything you made, plus a layered tiramisù and local wine.

experiences.name: Trastevere Twilight Supplì and Wine Crawl
experiences.description: Hop between an old bakery, a supplì fryer, a family salumeria and a candlelit wine bar just as the lanes fill for the evening. It's as much a lesson in Roman social life as it is a feast.

experiences.name: Vespa Sidecar Ride to the Appian Way Aqueducts
experiences.description: Climb into a vintage-style sidecar beside the Forum and ride out along the cobbled Appian Way, past catacombs and tombs, to the park where Roman aqueduct arches march across open fields. Your driver-guide stops for photos, espresso and a snack among the ruins.
